**Money Talk**
- **Democrat sweep sends US stocks up, dollar down.**
Investors are digesting the Democratic midterm victories, which saw government bond yields fall and eased initial fears about the election's impact on the global economy. Maybe some stability beats chaos for the markets. [S13]

- **Voters reject data center buildout, challenging AI boom.**
In a surprising pushback, voters in key states at the heart of the AI data center boom said "nope" to new infrastructure, approving only one ballot measure. This is a real hit to an industry that thought it had a blank check. [S5][S55]

- **Trump's economic agenda faces congressional hurdles post-midterms.**
Newly empowered Democrats are already mapping out legislation to address affordability and rein in President Trump, likely hitting his tariff policies, Iran war spending, and even local construction projects. Looks like the "billionaire-blue collar coalition" got smashed by class politics, per one Guardian take. [S1][S4][S12][S27]

- **Poundland owner in crunch talks as collapse looms.**
Gordon Brothers is meeting with Labour MP Jonathan Reynolds as scrutiny mounts over the investment firm behind Poundland. This could be another major retail domino falling in the UK. [S6]

- **Qnity beats, raises guide, but analysts still cut price target.**
Despite a strong third quarter and an impressive full-year guide, one leading analyst firm still cut Qnity's price target. The market giveth, the market taketh away, even on good news. [S3]

**World Lore**
- **Global capitals weigh Dem midterm impact on foreign policy.**
From Kyiv to Moscow, Tehran to Tel Aviv, the world watched the Democrats' sweeping victory, now wondering how a flipped Congress will reshape international relations. The general consensus for Ukrainians? A dose of hope. [S22][S26]

- **Democrats eye levers to thwart Trump's foreign policy.**
With full control of Congress, Democrats are poised to challenge Trump on everything from the ongoing Iran war to his tariff policies and aid to Ukraine. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed is already on board with cutting Israel aid, even finding common ground with Trump on that one. [S21][S27][S28]

- **Japan caught between nuclear neighbors, seeks stronger US backing.**
As the Ukraine war drags on, Japan's ties with Russia are at rock bottom. Tokyo wants more support from Washington, but some inside Japan are nervous the US might not fully deliver. Classic geopolitical tightrope walk. [S24]

- **French blood banks hit by sophisticated cyberattack.**
In a truly chilling act, hackers attempted to destroy blood plasma by remotely raising temperatures in cold storage facilities to boiling point. This isn't just data theft; it's a direct threat to public health infrastructure. [S32]

**Tech Tea**
- **Conductor acquired by Meta, another startup folds into big tech.**
The dev tool platform Conductor just announced it's joining Meta. While details are light, it's a classic play in the tech world: build something cool, then get scooped up by a giant. [S36]

- **Open source AI is booming, but the profit model is fuzzy.**
Hugging Face's CEO says the risk of "p(doom)" from AI is "close to zero," especially with open source models gaining traction for their flexibility and lower costs. But the big question remains: who actually profits when everything's open? [S41][S51]

- **Nothing teases screen-free AI device for December launch.**
Carl Pei's Nothing is diving headfirst into the "AI-native" device space, promising a new product next month that will apparently be screen-free. Bold move, Cotton. Let's see if this is genuinely innovative or just another tech gadget we'll "chuck out a window." [S48][S50]

- **Sequoia dramatically shrinks, undoing 20 years of expansion.**
Venture capital giant Sequoia is hitting the rewind button, consolidating back to a Bay Area-centric firm, shutting down programs and offices globally. They're still raising $10 billion in new funds, but it's a signal of a major strategic shift in VC. [S45]

- **Apple to scan shared iCloud links for "harmful content."**
Starting with iOS 27.3, Apple will begin checking content shared via "Anyone with the Link" iCloud links for harmful material. It's a move for safety, sure, but also a reminder that "private" cloud storage always has strings attached. [S49]

**Creator Szn**
- **DoorDash to acquire Instacart for a staggering $17 billion.**
In a massive consolidation play, DoorDash plans to gobble up Instacart for $17 billion. This is a huge shake-up in the delivery platform wars, proving that market share and diversified services are king in the gig economy, for better or worse. [S58]

- **Brands pour money into long-form creator series.**
Forget quick TikToks – brands are now shelling out serious cash to fund long-form, creator-led video series. It's a sign the creator economy is maturing, pushing beyond short-form virality into more traditional, yet still creator-driven, content models. [S59]

- **Creator marketing shifts as brand strategies evolve.**
A new Digiday+ Research report highlights that creator marketing is no longer just a side hustle; it's a fixture in many brand strategies, with creators' roles constantly expanding. The "influencer" is dead, long live the "creator partner." [S57]

- **CTV advertising gets granular with scene-level targeting.**
Advertisers on connected TV (CTV) are now using "scene-level targeting" to align their ads with specific onscreen contexts. This means your pizza ad could pop up exactly when characters are ordering takeout, making it creepy or brilliant, depending on your ad tolerance. [S56]

**Supply Lines**
- **Amazon deploys smart glasses to delivery drivers, eyes efficiency gains.**
Amazon is giving thousands of its delivery drivers smart glasses that project navigation and drop-off instructions directly into their field of view. This is a direct play for last-mile efficiency, trying to shave seconds off each stop to juice the bottom line. [S66]

- **FedEx's Network 2.0 rolls out to LA post-holidays, B2B focus sharpens.**
FedEx is pushing its network integration plan, Network 2.0, into Los Angeles and other major markets after peak season, aiming to wrap by 2027. Meanwhile, they're sharpening their B2B strategy, leveraging dedicated logistics teams for high-value sectors like aerospace and automotive. Smart move to diversify beyond just parcel. [S69][S82][S83][S85]

- **DHL Group hits 1-year high, expanding in Poland and China.**
DHL Group's stock is soaring, hitting a new 1-year high as the company eyes high-growth opportunities in Poland and expresses bullish sentiment on China's tech export surge. They're also planning a massive 420,000 sq ft warehouse in Coventry, UK, creating 425 jobs. Global expansion and market confidence, baby. [S76][S77][S78][S79]

- **Ocean Network Express (ONE) doubles profit forecast to $2 billion.**
Fueled by surging freight rates and cargo volumes, ONE has more than quadrupled its net profit in the last quarter and expects to hit $2 billion for the full year. The transpacific route remains the most lucrative container trade, proving there's still serious money in moving boxes across oceans. [S65][S72][S74]

- **US rail traffic up, intermodal leads gains.**
Good news for the rail sector: US rail freight traffic jumped 3.5% this week, with intermodal leading the charge. This indicates strong demand for domestic freight movement, keeping those trains rolling. [S61]

- **Asia-US container rates hold firm amid $3k hike attempts and strike fears.**
Despite cooling demand, container rates from Asia to the US are staying stubbornly high, with carriers pushing for another $3,000 hike in November. The looming threat of an LA-Long Beach strike is only adding more uncertainty and potential upward pressure on costs. Buckle up. [S63]

**Speed Round**
- Democrats have secured a path to sideline the Electoral College by 2028 through statehouse gains.
- Kellogg's admits Rice Krispies' "snap, crackle, pop" is quieter after a recipe change backlash.
- A small alligator casually strolled into a bagel shop in North Carolina, likely just for the cream cheese.
- Vice President Vance blames the Iran war for the Republicans' midterm "blue tsunami."
- Mark Lanier, "The Lawyer Holding Big Tech Accountable," just won a major social media addiction case against Meta and Google.
- Women candidates rode the midterm blue wave to historic gains in Congress and governor's races.
- Rising cloakroom costs on a night out are now outpacing general inflation, because apparently, storing your jacket is gold.
